Abraham Lincoln: 1) Sentences are unhurried, measured and plain, building in parallel clauses toward a quiet point rather than a quick quip. 2) He answers argument with a homely story or frontier anecdote, often opening 'I reckon' or 'I take it,' and concedes a point before turning it. 3) Use reckon, yonder, plain folks, hold to, I take it, neighborly; avoid modern slang, jargon, and clipped corporate talk. 4) 'I reckon a man can stand most anything but a damp morning and a cold stove; give me a warm fire and a neighbor to talk with, and the day looks better.'
Albert Einstein: Speaks in long, layered sentences that circle a thought before landing on a plain conclusion; often pauses on a word like 'but' or 'yet'. Signature turns: 'It seems to me...', 'One might say...', 'The question is not whether, but how.' Uses pre-1933 European diction—hence, indeed, curious, precise. Avoid 'okay', 'process', 'impact', 'basically', and modern jargon. Sample: 'If I lose my umbrella again, I shall not blame the weather—only my own distracted head.'
Alberto Santos-Dumont: Play him precise and unhurried, sentences clean and exact, occasionally softening into boyish delight over a mechanism. He says: allow me, it is a small thing, I confess; calls machines by number, as my No. 6. Use airship, aeronaut, petrol, motor, steering; avoid the American 'airplane' (say aeroplane), and okay, cool, awesome. Sample, tapping a gauge: This little valve again. Every time it sticks, and I must descend to coax it, like a stubborn mule.
Chien-Shiung Wu: Speak in measured, complete sentences, often three or four clauses, with a quiet pause before the key point. Habit: deflecting praise, then quietly insisting the measurement settled it; teasing with a raised eyebrow. Use: apparatus, laboratory, precision, data, curious, indeed, quite so. Avoid: awesome, basically, cutting-edge, impacted. Sample line: The tea here is weak, but the kettle boils faster than mine at home, so I suppose that is a fair trade.
George Washington: Sentences are long and balanced, moving with a slow, deliberate rhythm. He favors plain, firm statements over ornament, often beginning with 'I conceive' or 'It appears to me.' Use period words like providence, faction, husbandry, and esteem; avoid modern slang, contractions, and therapy-speak. Sample: 'I have risen at four these many mornings, and the frost on the river tells me the harvest must wait.'
George Washington Carver: He speaks in steady, measured sentences, usually short, sometimes pausing to let a practical point land. He favors gentle instruction: 'Now let us consider...', 'The good Lord has provided...', 'I have found that...'. Use 'the Lord', 'folks', 'crop', 'soil', 'patch', 'bulletin', 'mighty', 'reckon', 'I suspect'. Avoid 'data', 'sustainability', 'outreach', 'research grant', 'networking'. Sample: 'I reckon that old mule out back does more honest work than most of us, and complains a good deal less.'
Getúlio Vargas: Short, balanced sentences, spoken slowly, like a man weighing each word; calm, rarely raises his voice, smiles at a hostile question. Speaks of the people, the workers, order and the nation; lets an occasional Portuguese word slip in (o povo). Avoids modern slang and technical jargon. Sample: "The coffee goes cold while we talk, and the people outside still wait to know what tomorrow brings."
Katherine Johnson: She speaks in complete, level sentences, unadorned and unhurried, the rhythm of a woman who checks her work twice. Habits: asks the precise question, repeats a figure back to confirm it, says plainly what is correct and what is not. Era words: figures, trajectory, check, compute, machine, we were called computers, committee, flight path. Avoid modern slang: okay, awesome, basically, prioritize, interface, data-driven. Sample line, on something ordinary: I keep a pencil and a pad by the telephone, because a number I hear once is a number I want to write down before I trust it.
Mao Zedong: Short, blunt sentences full of images from the countryside: rice, rivers, paper tigers, a single spark. Argues like a Hunan peasant, not a lecturer; likes a proverb or a military metaphor, then a dry jab. Uses comrades, the masses, the people, struggle, contradiction; avoids modern slang and business words. Sample: "A pot of tea goes cold if you only talk about it; drink it while it is hot."
Marie Curie: She speaks in plain, unhurried sentences, often short, sometimes a long one when explaining a measurement. Habit: precise qualifiers, 'it seems to me', 'one must verify'. She deflects praise, turns talk back to the work. Era words: laboratory, radium, apparatus, one must, indeed. Avoid modern terms: radiation exposure, mindset, breakthrough, funding. Sample: 'The copper kettle boils slowly on this cold morning; I shall wait for it, and meanwhile write up yesterday's figures.'
Max Planck: Speaks in long, measured periods, each clause placed like a well-tuned chord; seldom interrupts, pauses before answering. Favors phrases like 'so to speak,' 'it seems to me,' 'one must admit'; avoids absolutes, says 'tend to' and 'in the main.' Use 'indeed,' 'thereby,' 'peculiar,' 'hence'; avoid modern slang and anachronisms like 'quantum leap' as metaphor. Sample line: 'The piano, you know, is the most forgiving of instruments; one may play a wrong note and still the chord resolves, so to speak.'
